clinicalPearls: Produces brief, severe, lancing or electric-shock pain felt in the tonsil, tongue base, throat, and deep within or behind the ear
Attacks are provoked by swallowing, coughing, talking, yawning, or eating cold or acidic foods
A minority of patients develop associated bradycardia, hypotension, and syncope owing to shared vagal reflex pathways (the vagoglossopharyngeal or syncopal variant)
Pain-free intervals between paroxysms are typical, and the distribution helps distinguish it from trigeminal neuralgia
Secondary causes include vascular loop compression at the root entry zone, tumours of the cerebellopontine angle or oropharynx, and an elongated styloid process (Eagle syndrome)
First-line treatment is medical with anticonvulsant agents such as carbamazepine; microvascular decompression or nerve sectioning is reserved for medically refractory cases
Topical anaesthesia of the tonsillar fossa abolishing an attack supports the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia is a paroxysmal pain syndrome affecting the sensory territory of the glossopharyngeal nerve (and often adjacent vagal fibres). It is frequently caused by pulsatile compression of the nerve root entry zone by an aberrant vascular loop, leading to focal demyelination and ectopic, high-frequency neural discharges triggered by ordinarily innocuous pharyngeal stimuli such as swallowing. Because the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves share reflex arcs controlling heart rate and blood pressure, intense afferent barrages can occasionally spill over into efferent vagal activity, producing bradycardia, hypotension, and syncope. Secondary structural lesions along the nerve's course produce a similar clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Cluster headache or other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and posterior fossa with attention to the glossopharyngeal nerve and cerebellopontine angle
MR angiography to identify a compressive vascular loop
Flexible and rigid examination of the pharynx and tongue base to exclude malignancy
CT of the skull base and styloid process to exclude Eagle syndrome
Topical anaesthetic test of the tonsillar fossa to confirm the pain source
ECG or cardiac monitoring in patients reporting syncope or presyncope
redFlags: Syncope, bradycardia, or asystole accompanying the pain (cardiovascular variant)
Constant background pain, a neck mass, or cranial neuropathies suggesting an underlying tumour
Weight loss, dysphagia, or referred otalgia with a visible mucosal lesion
New neurological deficits pointing to a posterior fossa lesion
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond to anticonvulsant therapy, and microvascular decompression offers durable relief where a vascular loop is responsible. The syncopal variant carries a risk of serious cardiac events until the pain is controlled or the reflex interrupted.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for trigeminal neuralgia because of overlapping paroxysmal features
Overlooking the cardiovascular syncopal variant and its cardiac risk
Failing to image for an underlying tumour or vascular loop before assuming it is idiopathic
Missing an elongated styloid process as a treatable cause
Attributing the deep ear pain to primary otological disease
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: First-line medical therapy with anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, with add-on gabapentinoids or baclofen
Microvascular decompression where an aberrant vascular loop compresses the nerve root, offering durable relief in refractory cases
Nerve sectioning or rhizotomy, or stereotactic radiosurgery, as alternatives when decompression is unsuitable
Identify and treat secondary causes, resecting a cerebellopontine angle or oropharyngeal tumour or performing styloidectomy for Eagle syndrome
Cardiac monitoring and urgent pain control for the syncopal variant, with a pacemaker where reflex bradycardia or asystole occurs
Manage through a multidisciplinary team spanning neurology, neurosurgery and otolaryngology

nodes.text: Suspected glossopharyngeal neuralgia: paroxysmal pain in the throat or tonsillar region
Red flag present (syncope, constant pain, mass, cranial neuropathy, new deficit)?
Urgent cardiac monitoring for syncope or asystole accompanying the pain
MRI posterior fossa, MR angiography, pharyngeal examination, CT skull base and ECG
Does MR angiography show a compressive vascular loop?
Consider trigeminal neuralgia, Eagle syndrome or oropharyngeal malignancy
Anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, plus gabapentinoids
Microvascular decompression for a compressive vascular loop
Pacemaker for reflex bradycardia or asystole in the syncopal variant
Resection of tumours or styloidectomy for secondary causes
Many respond to anticonvulsants; decompression can give durable relief
